label: Can speed priors yield deceptive models?

asks.author: evhub
asks.post_title: Are minimal circuits deceptive?
asks.statement: Prove whether time-complexity-biased (minimal circuit) models can be deceptive in the limit, as simplicity bias can.
asks.snippet: From a theoretical perspective, the two most natural types of inductive biases are simplicity bias and time complexity bias. Paul Christiano has previously argued that simplicity bias can be deceptive in the limit, but left the question of whether the same is true of time complexity bias as an open problem. The goal of this post is to attempt to resolve that open problem.

asks.snippet: That is because, between the models that are capable of deception, the ones with less complex (unaligned) objectives are simpler than the aligned ones which have a more complex objective. He then left the open question of whether penalizing time complexity can lead to a deceptive model or not. Deceptive models have a particular property: they need to spend time figuring out if they are out of the training or not.

One of the most persuasive arguments that alignment may be extremely hard has always been that we have to get it right on the first critical try (the word ‘critical’ is doing quite a lot of work here: it’s being used to mean “clearly existentially disastrous if failed” — which is a real thing, for AI Alignment).

Whether this is enough data to learn robust regulatory representations, or whether the perturbation signal will be drowned out by the much larger observational pretraining corpus, is an open empirical question, but I think my other research on scaling laws for biological foundation models may shed some light on it. 7.2.

label: Radical flank effect of pause advocacy
statement: Measure whether radical AI pause advocacy or framing produces net safety gains through radical flank effects, versus harms to advocates.

asks.author: Thomas Kwa
asks.statement: Study the radical flank effect of AI pause advocacy to determine whether the advocacy is net good or bad.
asks.snippet: I now think the majority of impact of AI pause advocacy will come from the radical flank effect, and people should study it to decide whether pause advocacy is good or bad.

asks.author: Gabriel Alfour
asks.post_title: It will cost you nothing to "bribe" a Utilitarian
asks.statement: Study whether calling an AI pause 'radical' earns lab leaders credibility that yields a larger safety premium, outweighing harms to pause advocates.
asks.snippet: Depicting an AI Pause as "Radical" (Buck [2025]) or "Most Extreme" (Dario [2023]) often confers credibility that allows individuals to maintain influence across multiple stakeholder groups. It would be interesting to study whether such credibility translates into a higher safety premium than the usual ϵ/k, and whether this dominates the negative effects of shooting down pause advocates. Social enforcement and peer dynamics.

label: Selective attack timing in control evals
statement: Evaluate control protocols against attack policies that choose when to attack, and measure models' attack-selection ability.

asks.author: Mia Hopman
asks.post_title: Untrusted AIs can exploit feedback in control protocols
asks.statement: Evaluate feedback-based control protocols against red-team attack policies that selectively choose when to insert backdoors rather than always attacking.
asks.snippet: Variable attack insertion strategies represent a critical methodological improvement, as current evaluations rely on scenarios where attack policies always attempt backdoor insertion. Future work should examine selective attack strategies where red teams choose when to attack, better approximating real-world threat models where scheming models might only rarely attempt subversion, and aligning methodology with established safety definitions used in other control protocol evaluations. Automated auditing strategies could deliberately exploit feedback interactions to collect evidence of malicious intent rather than focusing solely on output improvement.

asks.author: J Bostock
asks.statement: Measure how well untrusted AI models perform attack selection in the untrusted-monitoring control setup.
asks.snippet: We (roughly) ended up concluding that there are three really big questions in the textbook untrusted monitoring setup, and only one of them (measuring how good your AI is at recognising its own attacks, as opposed to honeypots) has really been addressed in the major control papers. The other two problems are what to do when you catch your AI doing something bad, which has been discussed informally in Redwood's blogposts but mostly, and how to measure your AI's attack selection, which basically hasn't been studied.

label: Do steering effects transfer across models?
statement: Test whether steering vectors and their effects transfer across architectures, sizes, and MoE models.

asks.author: Moksh Nirvaan
asks.post_title: Probing Power-Seeking in LLMs
asks.statement: Test whether power-seeking steering vector effects persist across different LLM architectures and sizes and across broader layer sets.
asks.snippet: This narrow layer selection likely captures only a subset of the model’s full representational space for the targeted trait, meaning we may be steering through just one of several possible control points for manipulative or power-seeking behavior. Future work could expand this analysis by extracting and testing analogous vectors across a broader set of layers and, importantly, evaluating whether these effects persist across different model architectures and sizes. Such cross-model experiments would help determine whether the behaviors we observe here reflect idiosyncrasies of this fine-tuned model or a more generalizable phenomenon in large language models.

asks.author: niklas_herbster
asks.post_title: Restoring Model Alignment via Honesty Activation Steering
asks.statement: Test whether honesty activation steering methods and directions transfer to Mixture-of-Experts models.
asks.snippet: Do our methods also transfer to Mixture-of-Expert models? Our current experiments are limited to dense architectures and it remains an open problem whether our presented methods and our steering directions transfer to MoE models. Stability of the direction.

label: Is AI 2027 tracking reality?
statement: Compare actual AI progress, such as METR horizon growth, against the AI 2027 scenario's forecast timeline and quantify the gap.

asks.author: Daniel Kokotajlo
asks.statement: Quantify how actual AI progress since publication compares to the AI 2027 scenario's predicted timeline.
asks.snippet: My general sense right now is that progress has been somewhat slower than AI 2027 expected, and even slower than I expected at the time (my median was 2028 at the time) but not dramatically slower. It would be good to quantify this.

asks.author: titotal
asks.post_title: A deep critique of AI 2027’s bad timeline models
asks.statement: Validate the AI 2027 timeline models against actual observed data, e.g. compare forecasts with realized METR horizon growth.
asks.snippet: I'm not super excited about revisiting the model, to be honest, but I'll probably take a look at some point. What I'd really like to see, and what I haven't noticed from a quick look through the update, is some attempt to prove the validity of the models with reference to actual data. For example, I think METR comes off looking pretty good right now with their exponential model of horizon growth, which has held up for nearly a year post-publication now.

label: How long do centaur periods last?
statement: Measure the duration and trajectory of human-AI centaur/cyborg periods across domains like chess, Go, poker and classification.

asks.author: Tomáš Gavenčiak
asks.post_title: Cyborg Periods: There will be multiple AI transitions
asks.statement: Model and measure the trajectory of human-AI cyborg periods across domains to find common transition dynamics.
asks.snippet: This is likely relatively tractable and would be informative for prediction of future development of the transitions. While the dynamic would differ between domains (not just the current stage but also the overall trajectory shape), I would expect some common dynamics that would be interesting to explore and model. A few examples of concrete questions that could be tractable today:

asks.author: niplav
asks.statement: Measure the human-AI centaur gap duration in poker, Go, checkers, image classification, speech recognition and GPQA.
asks.snippet: This centaur gap might be effectively zero in some domains such as arithmetic, and lasted ~14 years/<1 economic doubling/<10 compute doublings in chess. I'd like to see investigations for the centaur gap of poker, Go, checkers, image classification, speech recognition, GPQA… This can be relevant in cases with a "controlled intelligence explosion" where humans adjust the process along the way: this process can only go on as long as the resulting AI systems are not efficient with respect to humans.

label: Timelines under higher brain-compute estimates
statement: Recompute AI timeline forecasts assuming brain compute is orders of magnitude higher than standard estimates (e.g., microtubules, per-neuron ANN costs).

asks.author: kokotajlod
asks.post_title: It takes 5 layers and 1000 artificial neurons to simulate a single biological neuron [Link]
asks.statement: Calculate how a ~1000-neuron-ANN-per-biological-neuron compute requirement shifts AI timeline estimates, e.g. probability of <15 and >30 year timelines.
asks.snippet: (Plausibly we'll be able to find more efficient ways to simulate neurons than the dumb 8-layer NN they tried in this paper, shaving an OOM or so off the cost, bringing us back down to 10^16again...) It's unclear whether this would lengthen or shorten timelines, I'd like to see the calculations for that. My wild guess is that it would lower the probability of <15 year timelines and also lower the probability of >30 year timelines.

asks.author: tula
asks.post_title: Counterarguments to the basic AI x-risk case
asks.statement: Recompute AI timeline projections assuming brain microtubules perform computation, raising brain compute estimates by three orders of magnitude.
asks.snippet: If microtubule lattices are storing or calculating information, it implies that the brain is actually calculating at least \emph{three magnitudes larger} bits of info per second than previously thought with a stunning level of parallelization & connectivity. This sets the bar for human-level intelligence significantly higher, and I would be very interested to see how much this affects growth projections that get tossed around & the confidence assigned to said projections.

asks.snippet: On the other hand, nuclear weapons are widely considered a huge deal, and were a big discontinuity. It would be nice to check this more systematically. IV.

label: AI risk schools of thought
statement: Identify schools of thought among AI risk skeptics and concerned forecasters and test how their stories affect their forecasts.

asks.author: Forecasting Research Institute
asks.post_title: Results from an Adversarial Collaboration on AI Risk (FRI)
asks.statement: Identify schools of thought among AI risk skeptics and concerned forecasters and test how their stories affect their forecasts.
asks.snippet: The skeptic and concerned groups are not monoliths – within each group, people disagree about what the most likely AI dangers are, in addition to how likely those dangers are to happen. Future work could try to find these schools of thought and see how their stories do or do not affect their forecasts. Would future adversarial collaborations be more successful if they focused on a smaller number of participants who work particularly well together and provided them with teams of researchers and other aids to support them?

label: Returns to LLM scaffolding investment
statement: Measure the returns curve to investment in LLM scaffolding, including recursive scaffolding improvement by language models.

asks.author: Owen Cotton-Barratt
asks.post_title: On the future of language models
asks.statement: Measure the returns curve to investment in improving LLM scaffolding, including recursive scaffolding self-improvement.
asks.snippet: Scaffolding is a language-based construction, so language models could plausibly learn how to contribute to better scaffolding (which can then be experimented with, and could recursively feed into further improvements to scaffolding). We are therefore interested in a question like “what is the returns curve to investment on improving scaffolding?”, which is an empirical question. For some possible shapes of the curve, improvements to scaffolding could precipitate an intelligence explosion, gathering pace faster and faster as successive generations of scaffolding are more effective than the last at further improving the scaffolding.

label: When does narrow-to-broad generalization occur?
statement: Fine-tune LLMs on narrow domains and measure broad generalization across model sizes and train-eval domain distances.

asks.author: Valerio Pepe
asks.post_title: [CS 2881r] Some Generalizations of Emergent Misalignment
asks.statement: Test how benign-finetuning-induced broad alignment generalization varies with LLM size and with distance between training and evaluation domains.
asks.snippet: Thus, we can consider this experiment successful; it’s possible to induce broad alignment in models by finetuning them on a benign dataset for some domain X, and measuring an increase in alignment on some other domain Y. Future work could explore how this phenomenon changes across different LLM sizes, or across domains that are closer together/farther apart than the ones used here[3]. Inducing Behavioral Shifts with Mundane Data

asks.author: Jorio Cocola
asks.post_title: Weird Generalization & Inductive Backdoors
asks.statement: Run extensive fine-tuning experiments to determine under what conditions narrow-to-broad generalization occurs in LLMs.
asks.snippet: Instead, we provide a few concrete cases of narrow-to-broad generalization. Future work could investigate under what conditions narrow-to-broad generalization occurs by doing extensive experiments. We think giving a general predictive theory may be difficult.

label: Relax debate stability assumption
statement: Modify prover-estimator debate to relax or weaken its stability and independent-evidence assumptions, and prove it still works.

asks.author: Marie_DB
asks.post_title: An alignment safety case sketch based on debate
asks.statement: Modify prover-estimator debate to relax the stability assumption and prove it still works, e.g. via honesty-focused objectives.
asks.snippet: But stability might not hold for relevant queries. Future work could modify prover-estimator debate to relax the stability assumption, for example by focusing on honesty instead of correctness or by transforming an unstable computation into a stable one. Avoids gerrymandering concerns: Debate protocols such as cross-examination punish debaters for inconsistency across claims at the same recursive level.

asks.author: Jonah Brown-Cohen
asks.post_title:
Prover-Estimator Debate: 
A New Scalable Oversight Protocol
asks.statement: Prove whether stable arguments exist for prover-estimator debate under weaker assumptions than sufficient independent evidence.
asks.snippet: For example, if a human judge is given three pieces of evidence for a claim, can they accurately say whether the truth-values of each piece of evidence are independent? Thus we have two key open problems: a theoretical question of whether stable arguments exist under weaker assumptions than sufficient independent evidence, and an empirical question about when we can find independent evidence in practice.
